title: Guido van Rossum and the Christmas Origins of Python (1989)
explainer: Python began as Guido van Rossum's personal project during a week off at the end of December 1989 at a Dutch research institute, and he released it publicly in 1991. He named it after the British comedy troupe Monty Python rather than the snake — by his own account the choice had nothing to do with reptiles — and the same taste for plainness over ceremony shows up in the dunder-method design this lesson covers: ordinary syntax like len(obj) or for x in obj reads naturally instead of requiring a formal interface declaration.

title: PEP 318 and the Contentious Birth of the Decorator (2003-2004)
explainer: The @decorator syntax this lesson teaches wasn't an obvious design choice: it came out of PEP 318, proposed in mid-2003 to let a function be transformed — made a classmethod, timed, retried — right at its declaration instead of by reassigning it afterward. The proposal spent more than a year in public argument on Python's mailing lists over syntax and scope before being finalized for Python 2.4 in late 2004, a useful reminder that syntax you now type without thinking was, at the time, genuinely controversial.
